#### ! Scenario

*Or what to do when excluding a dependency fixes the build but breaks runtime*
This scenario demonstrates how to surgically remove a transitive dependency from the graph.

This is a common "sledgehammer" fix for conflicts.

::: {.callout-note title="Tool Versions"}
This scenario was tested with **Maven 3.9**; the behaviour shown applies to Maven 3.x.
:::

#### ! Example

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 4.4
graph LR
    Root[Project Root] --> LibA[lib-a:1.0.0]
    LibA --> LibB[lib-b:1.0.0]
    LibB -.-> LibC[lib-c:1.0.0]
    Root -- excludes from lib-a --> LibC
```

```{.xml include="pom.xml" snippet="s5-deps"}
```

#### ! Expect
Excluding `lib-c` removes it and its transitive subtree from the graph entirely.

#### ! Actual
`lib-c` is gone from this path. `lib-b`, which is the artifact that actually asked for it, is still present and still expects `lib-c` to be on the classpath at runtime.

#### ! Why
An `<exclusion>` is metadata on one dependency edge. While traversing `lib-a`'s subtree, Maven drops any node matching the excluded coordinates, however deep it sits. It applies to that declaration only: if another direct dependency also pulls in `lib-c`, it comes back through that path ([MS18](../scenario-18-banning/guide.qmd)).

#### ! Fix
This *is* the fix for many problems (for example, excluding `commons-logging` to route logging through SLF4J). Pair it with one of:

*   **A replacement:** declare the library that provides the same classes ([MS15](../scenario-15-substitution/guide.qmd)).
*   **A test run:** exercise the code paths in `lib-b` that used `lib-c`, because the compiler will not tell you they are broken.

#### ! Risk
* LOW Replacing an implementation (for example `log4j` with `logback` plus a bridge).
* MEDIUM Excluding a transitive you believe is unused; future versions may require it.
* HIGH Excluding to "fix" a conflict without understanding the dependency; this frequently causes `NoClassDefFoundError` at runtime.

#### ! Check

**Fast check:** `mvn dependency:tree`

**What to look for:** `lib-c` absent under `lib-a` (and under `lib-b`). If it remains elsewhere in the tree, another path is pulling it in.

**Conclusion:** The exclusion successfully prunes the dependency from this path.

#### ! Scales
Overuse of exclusions leads to "Swiss cheese" dependency graphs that are hard to reason about.

#### ! Takeaway
Exclusions remove a library from the graph, not from the code that calls it. Use them only when you know the dependent library can function without the excluded artifact, or you are providing a replacement.

#### ! Related
*   [MS15](../scenario-15-substitution/guide.qmd) - Replacing a library instead of just removing it.
*   [MS18](../scenario-18-banning/guide.qmd) - Keeping an artifact out of the whole build, not just one path.
*   [GS5](../../gradle-demo/scenario-5-exclusions/guide.qmd) - The same exclusion in Gradle.
*   [SB5](../../sbt-demo/scenario-5-exclusions/guide.qmd) - The same exclusion in sbt.
*   [P9](../../python-demo/scenario-9-exclusions-gap/guide.qmd) - Python, where pip and Poetry have no exclusion at all and only uv can remove a transitive.

#### ! Wild

For years, the most common use of exclusions in the Java ecosystem was logging. Prior to Spring Framework 5, any project that wanted to use SLF4J had to explicitly exclude `commons-logging` from Spring's transitive dependencies, a pattern so widespread that Spring's own [blog documented the problem](https://spring.io/blog/2009/12/04/logging-dependencies-in-spring/) and the [SLF4J FAQ](https://www.slf4j.org/faq.html) devoted a section to it. Spring eventually solved it in 5.0 by replacing `commons-logging` with its own [`spring-jcl` bridge module](https://docs.spring.io/spring-framework/reference/core/spring-jcl.html). The logging exclusion pattern remains common in projects that consolidate multiple logging frameworks (excluding `log4j` in favour of `logback`, or removing `slf4j-simple` to prevent binding conflicts).

License compliance scans do frequently uncover GPL-licensed libraries pulled in transitively. However, the fix is rarely as simple as excluding and substituting; permissively licensed drop-in replacements with compatible APIs are uncommon. More often, teams must get legal to approve the transitive inclusion, restructure the code to avoid the dependency entirely, or accept the license obligation.
